nodes.Name: Time
nodes.DocComment:
A Time represents an instant in time with nanosecond precision.

Programs using times should typically store and pass them as values,
not pointers. That is, time variables and struct fields should be of
type [time.Time], not *time.Time.

A Time value can be used by multiple goroutines simultaneously except
that the methods [Time.GobDecode], [Time.UnmarshalBinary], [Time.UnmarshalJSON] and
[Time.UnmarshalText] are not concurrency-safe.

Time instants can be compared using the [Time.Before], [Time.After], and [Time.Equal] methods.
The [Time.Sub] method subtracts two instants, producing a [Duration].
The [Time.Add] method adds a Time and a Duration, producing a Time.

The zero value of type Time is January 1, year 1, 00:00:00.000000000 UTC.
As this time is unlikely to come up in practice, the [Time.IsZero] method gives
a simple way of detecting a time that has not been initialized explicitly.

Each time has an associated [Location]. The methods [Time.Local], [Time.UTC], and Time.In return a
Time with a specific Location. Changing the Location of a Time value with
these methods does not change the actual instant it represents, only the time
zone in which to interpret it.

Representations of a Time value saved by the [Time.GobEncode], [Time.MarshalBinary], [Time.AppendBinary],
[Time.MarshalJSON], [Time.MarshalText] and [Time.AppendText] methods store the [Time.Location]'s offset,
but not the location name. They therefore lose information about Daylight Saving Time.

In addition to the required “wall clock” reading, a Time may contain an optional
reading of the current process's monotonic clock, to provide additional precision
for comparison or subtraction.
See the “Monotonic Clocks” section in the package documentation for details.

Note that the Go == operator compares not just the time instant but also the
Location and the monotonic clock reading. Therefore, Time values should not
be used as map or database keys without first guaranteeing that the
identical Location has been set for all values, which can be achieved
through use of the UTC or Local method, and that the monotonic clock reading
has been stripped by setting t = t.Round(0). In general, prefer t.Equal(u)
to t == u, since t.Equal uses the most accurate comparison available and
correctly handles the case when only one of its arguments has a monotonic
clock reading.

nodes.Name: nsec
nodes.DocComment: nsec returns the time's nanoseconds.

nodes.Name: sec
nodes.DocComment: sec returns the time's seconds since Jan 1 year 1.

nodes.Name: unixSec
nodes.DocComment: unixSec returns the time's seconds since Jan 1 1970 (Unix time).

nodes.Name: addSec
nodes.DocComment: addSec adds d seconds to the time.

nodes.Name: setLoc
nodes.DocComment: setLoc sets the location associated with the time.

nodes.Name: stripMono
nodes.DocComment: stripMono strips the monotonic clock reading in t.

nodes.Name: setMono
nodes.DocComment:
setMono sets the monotonic clock reading in t.
If t cannot hold a monotonic clock reading,
because its wall time is too large,
setMono is a no-op.

nodes.Name: mono
nodes.DocComment:
mono returns t's monotonic clock reading.
It returns 0 for a missing reading.
This function is used only for testing,
so it's OK that technically 0 is a valid
monotonic clock reading as well.

nodes.Name: IsZero
nodes.DocComment:
IsZero reports whether t represents the zero time instant,
January 1, year 1, 00:00:00 UTC.

nodes.Name: After
nodes.DocComment: After reports whether the time instant t is after u.

nodes.Name: Before
nodes.DocComment: Before reports whether the time instant t is before u.

nodes.Name: Compare
nodes.DocComment:
Compare compares the time instant t with u. If t is before u, it returns -1;
if t is after u, it returns +1; if they're the same, it returns 0.

nodes.Name: Equal
nodes.DocComment:
Equal reports whether t and u represent the same time instant.
Two times can be equal even if they are in different locations.
For example, 6:00 +0200 and 4:00 UTC are Equal.
See the documentation on the Time type for the pitfalls of using == with
Time values; most code should use Equal instead.

nodes.Name: Month
nodes.DocComment: A Month specifies a month of the year (January = 1, ...).

nodes.Name: String
nodes.DocComment: String returns the English name of the month ("January", "February", ...).

nodes.Name: Weekday
nodes.DocComment: A Weekday specifies a day of the week (Sunday = 0, ...).

nodes.Name: String
nodes.DocComment: String returns the English name of the day ("Sunday", "Monday", ...).

absSeconds
nodes.DocComment: An absSeconds counts the number of seconds since the absolute zero instant.

nodes.Name: absDays
nodes.DocComment: An absDays counts the number of days since the absolute zero instant.

nodes.Name: absCentury
nodes.DocComment: An absCentury counts the number of centuries since the absolute zero instant.

nodes.Name: absCyear
nodes.DocComment: An absCyear counts the number of years since the start of a century.

nodes.Name: absYday
nodes.DocComment:
An absYday counts the number of days since the start of a year.
Note that absolute years start on March 1.

nodes.Name: absMonth
nodes.DocComment:
An absMonth counts the number of months since the start of a year.
absMonth=0 denotes March.

nodes.Name: absLeap
nodes.DocComment: An absLeap is a single bit (0 or 1) denoting whether a given year is a leap year.

nodes.Name: absJanFeb
nodes.DocComment:
An absJanFeb is a single bit (0 or 1) denoting whether a given day falls in January or February.
That is a special case because the absolute years start in March (unlike normal calendar years).

nodes.Name: dateToAbsDays
nodes.DocComment:
dateToAbsDays takes a standard year/month/day and returns the
number of days from the absolute epoch to that day.
The days argument can be out of range and in particular can be negative.

nodes.Name: days
nodes.DocComment: days converts absolute seconds to absolute days.

nodes.Name: split
nodes.DocComment: split splits days into century, cyear, ayday.

nodes.Name: split
nodes.DocComment: split splits ayday into absolute month and standard (1-based) day-in-month.

nodes.Name: janFeb
nodes.DocComment: janFeb returns 1 if the March 1-based ayday is in January or February, 0 otherwise.

nodes.Name: month
nodes.DocComment: month returns the standard Month for (m, janFeb)

nodes.Name: leap
nodes.DocComment: leap returns 1 if (century, cyear) is a leap year, 0 otherwise.

nodes.Name: year
nodes.DocComment: year returns the standard year for (century, cyear, janFeb).

nodes.Name: yday
nodes.DocComment: yday returns the standard 1-based yday for (ayday, janFeb, leap).

nodes.Name: date
nodes.DocComment: date converts days into standard year, month, day.

nodes.Name: yearYday
nodes.DocComment: yearYday converts days into the standard year and 1-based yday.

nodes.Name: absSec
nodes.DocComment:
absSec returns the time t as an absolute seconds, adjusted by the zone offset.
It is called when computing a presentation property like Month or Hour.
We'd rather call it abs, but there are linknames to abs that make that problematic.
See timeAbs below.

Children.Name: if
Children.RawSource: l.cacheZone != nil && l.cacheStart <= sec && sec < l.cacheEnd

nodes.Name: locabs
nodes.DocComment:
locabs is a combination of the Zone and abs methods,
extracting both return values from a single zone lookup.

Children.Name: if
Children.RawSource: l.cacheZone != nil && l.cacheStart <= sec && sec < l.cacheEnd

nodes.Name: Date
nodes.DocComment: Date returns the year, month, and day in which t occurs.

nodes.Name: Year
nodes.DocComment: Year returns the year in which t occurs.

nodes.Name: Month
nodes.DocComment: Month returns the month of the year specified by t.

nodes.Name: Day
nodes.DocComment: Day returns the day of the month specified by t.

nodes.Name: Weekday
nodes.DocComment: Weekday returns the day of the week specified by t.

nodes.Name: weekday
nodes.DocComment: weekday returns the day of the week specified by days.

nodes.Name: ISOWeek
nodes.DocComment:
ISOWeek returns the ISO 8601 year and week number in which t occurs.
Week ranges from 1 to 53. Jan 01 to Jan 03 of year n might belong to
week 52 or 53 of year n-1, and Dec 29 to Dec 31 might belong to week 1
of year n+1.

nodes.Name: Clock
nodes.DocComment: Clock returns the hour, minute, and second within the day specified by t.

nodes.Name: clock
nodes.DocComment: clock returns the hour, minute, and second within the day specified by abs.

nodes.Name: Hour
nodes.DocComment: Hour returns the hour within the day specified by t, in the range [0, 23].

nodes.Name: Minute
nodes.DocComment: Minute returns the minute offset within the hour specified by t, in the range [0, 59].

nodes.Name: Second
nodes.DocComment: Second returns the second offset within the minute specified by t, in the range [0, 59].

nodes.Name: Nanosecond
nodes.DocComment:
Nanosecond returns the nanosecond offset within the second specified by t,
in the range [0, 999999999].

nodes.Name: YearDay
nodes.DocComment:
YearDay returns the day of the year specified by t, in the range [1,365] for non-leap years,
and [1,366] in leap years.

nodes.Name: Duration
nodes.DocComment:
A Duration represents the elapsed time between two instants
as an int64 nanosecond count. The representation limits the
largest representable duration to approximately 290 years.

nodes.Name: Nanosecond
nodes.DocComment:
Common durations. There is no definition for units of Day or larger
to avoid confusion across daylight savings time zone transitions.

To count the number of units in a [Duration], divide:

	second := time.Second
	fmt.Print(int64(second/time.Millisecond)) // prints 1000

To convert an integer number of units to a Duration, multiply:

	seconds := 10
	fmt.Print(time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second) // prints 10s

nodes.Name: String
nodes.DocComment:
String returns a string representing the duration in the form "72h3m0.5s".
Leading zero units are omitted. As a special case, durations less than one
second format use a smaller unit (milli-, micro-, or nanoseconds) to ensure
that the leading digit is non-zero. The zero duration formats as 0s.

nodes.Name: format
nodes.DocComment:
format formats the representation of d into the end of buf and
returns the offset of the first character.

nodes.Name: fmtFrac
nodes.DocComment:
fmtFrac formats the fraction of v/10**prec (e.g., ".12345") into the
tail of buf, omitting trailing zeros. It omits the decimal
point too when the fraction is 0. It returns the index where the
output bytes begin and the value v/10**prec.

nodes.Name: fmtInt
nodes.DocComment:
fmtInt formats v into the tail of buf.
It returns the index where the output begins.

nodes.Name: Nanoseconds
nodes.DocComment: Nanoseconds returns the duration as an integer nanosecond count.

nodes.Name: Microseconds
nodes.DocComment: Microseconds returns the duration as an integer microsecond count.

nodes.Name: Milliseconds
nodes.DocComment: Milliseconds returns the duration as an integer millisecond count.

nodes.Name: Seconds
nodes.DocComment: Seconds returns the duration as a floating point number of seconds.

nodes.Name: Minutes
nodes.DocComment: Minutes returns the duration as a floating point number of minutes.

nodes.Name: Hours
nodes.DocComment: Hours returns the duration as a floating point number of hours.

nodes.Name: Truncate
nodes.DocComment:
Truncate returns the result of rounding d toward zero to a multiple of m.
If m <= 0, Truncate returns d unchanged.

nodes.Name: lessThanHalf
nodes.DocComment:
lessThanHalf reports whether x+x < y but avoids overflow,
assuming x and y are both positive (Duration is signed).

nodes.Name: Round
nodes.DocComment:
Round returns the result of rounding d to the nearest multiple of m.
The rounding behavior for halfway values is to round away from zero.
If the result exceeds the maximum (or minimum)
value that can be stored in a [Duration],
Round returns the maximum (or minimum) duration.
If m <= 0, Round returns d unchanged.

nodes.Name: Abs
nodes.DocComment:
Abs returns the absolute value of d.
As a special case, Duration([math.MinInt64]) is converted to Duration([math.MaxInt64]),
reducing its magnitude by 1 nanosecond.

nodes.Name: Add
nodes.DocComment: Add returns the time t+d.

Children.Name: if
Children.RawSource: d < 0 && te > t.ext || d > 0 && te < t.ext

nodes.Name: Sub
nodes.DocComment:
Sub returns the duration t-u. If the result exceeds the maximum (or minimum)
value that can be stored in a [Duration], the maximum (or minimum) duration
will be returned.
To compute t-d for a duration d, use t.Add(-d).

nodes.Name: Since
nodes.DocComment:
Since returns the time elapsed since t.
It is shorthand for time.Now().Sub(t).

nodes.Name: Until
nodes.DocComment:
Until returns the duration until t.
It is shorthand for t.Sub(time.Now()).

nodes.Name: AddDate
nodes.DocComment:
AddDate returns the time corresponding to adding the
given number of years, months, and days to t.
For example, AddDate(-1, 2, 3) applied to January 1, 2011
returns March 4, 2010.

Note that dates are fundamentally coupled to timezones, and calendrical
periods like days don't have fixed durations. AddDate uses the Location of
the Time value to determine these durations. That means that the same
AddDate arguments can produce a different shift in absolute time depending on
the base Time value and its Location. For example, AddDate(0, 0, 1) applied
to 12:00 on March 27 always returns 12:00 on March 28. At some locations and
in some years this is a 24 hour shift. In others it's a 23 hour shift due to
daylight savings time transitions.

AddDate normalizes its result in the same way that Date does,
so, for example, adding one month to October 31 yields
December 1, the normalized form for November 31.

nodes.Name: daysBefore
nodes.DocComment:
daysBefore returns the number of days in a non-leap year before month m.
daysBefore(December+1) returns 365.

nodes.Name: now
nodes.DocComment:
Provided by package runtime.

now returns the current real time, and is superseded by runtimeNow which returns
the fake synctest clock when appropriate.

now should be an internal detail,
but widely used packages access it using linkname.
Notable members of the hall of shame include:
  - gitee.com/quant1x/gox
  - github.com/phuslu/log
  - github.com/sethvargo/go-limiter
  - github.com/ulule/limiter/v3

Do not remove or change the type signature.
See go.dev/issue/67401.

nodes.Name: runtimeNow
nodes.DocComment:
runtimeNow returns the current time.
When called within a synctest.Run bubble, it returns the group's fake clock.

go:linkname runtimeNow

nodes.Name: runtimeNano
nodes.DocComment:
runtimeNano returns the current value of the runtime clock in nanoseconds.
When called within a synctest.Run bubble, it returns the group's fake clock.

go:linkname runtimeNano

nodes.Name: runtimeIsBubbled
nodes.DocComment: go:linkname runtimeIsBubbled

nodes.Name: startNano
nodes.DocComment:
Monotonic times are reported as offsets from startNano.
We initialize startNano to runtimeNano() - 1 so that on systems where
monotonic time resolution is fairly low (e.g. Windows 2008
which appears to have a default resolution of 15ms),
we avoid ever reporting a monotonic time of 0.
(Callers may want to use 0 as "time not set".)

nodes.Name: Now
nodes.DocComment: Now returns the current local time.

nodes.Name: UTC
nodes.DocComment: UTC returns t with the location set to UTC.

nodes.Name: Local
nodes.DocComment: Local returns t with the location set to local time.

nodes.Name: In
nodes.DocComment:
In returns a copy of t representing the same time instant, but
with the copy's location information set to loc for display
purposes.

In panics if loc is nil.

nodes.Name: Location
nodes.DocComment: Location returns the time zone information associated with t.

nodes.Name: Zone
nodes.DocComment:
Zone computes the time zone in effect at time t, returning the abbreviated
name of the zone (such as "CET") and its offset in seconds east of UTC.

nodes.Name: ZoneBounds
nodes.DocComment:
ZoneBounds returns the bounds of the time zone in effect at time t.
The zone begins at start and the next zone begins at end.
If the zone begins at the beginning of time, start will be returned as a zero Time.
If the zone goes on forever, end will be returned as a zero Time.
The Location of the returned times will be the same as t.

nodes.Name: Unix
nodes.DocComment:
Unix returns t as a Unix time, the number of seconds elapsed
since January 1, 1970 UTC. The result does not depend on the
location associated with t.
Unix-like operating systems often record time as a 32-bit
count of seconds, but since the method here returns a 64-bit
value it is valid for billions of years into the past or future.

nodes.Name: UnixMilli
nodes.DocComment:
UnixMilli returns t as a Unix time, the number of milliseconds elapsed since
January 1, 1970 UTC. The result is undefined if the Unix time in
milliseconds cannot be represented by an int64 (a date more than 292 million
years before or after 1970). The result does not depend on the
location associated with t.

nodes.Name: UnixMicro
nodes.DocComment:
UnixMicro returns t as a Unix time, the number of microseconds elapsed since
January 1, 1970 UTC. The result is undefined if the Unix time in
microseconds cannot be represented by an int64 (a date before year -290307 or
after year 294246). The result does not depend on the location associated
with t.

nodes.Name: UnixNano
nodes.DocComment:
UnixNano returns t as a Unix time, the number of nanoseconds elapsed
since January 1, 1970 UTC. The result is undefined if the Unix time
in nanoseconds cannot be represented by an int64 (a date before the year
1678 or after 2262). Note that this means the result of calling UnixNano
on the zero Time is undefined. The result does not depend on the
location associated with t.

nodes.Name: AppendBinary
nodes.DocComment: AppendBinary implements the [encoding.BinaryAppender] interface.

nodes.Name: MarshalBinary
nodes.DocComment: MarshalBinary implements the [encoding.BinaryMarshaler] interface.

nodes.Name: UnmarshalBinary
nodes.DocComment: UnmarshalBinary implements the [encoding.BinaryUnmarshaler] interface.

nodes.Name: GobEncode
nodes.DocComment: GobEncode implements the gob.GobEncoder interface.

nodes.Name: GobDecode
nodes.DocComment: GobDecode implements the gob.GobDecoder interface.

nodes.Name: MarshalJSON
nodes.DocComment:
MarshalJSON implements the [encoding/json.Marshaler] interface.
The time is a quoted string in the RFC 3339 format with sub-second precision.
If the timestamp cannot be represented as valid RFC 3339
(e.g., the year is out of range), then an error is reported.

nodes.Name: UnmarshalJSON
nodes.DocComment:
UnmarshalJSON implements the [encoding/json.Unmarshaler] interface.
The time must be a quoted string in the RFC 3339 format.

nodes.Name: AppendText
nodes.DocComment:
AppendText implements the [encoding.TextAppender] interface.
The time is formatted in RFC 3339 format with sub-second precision.
If the timestamp cannot be represented as valid RFC 3339
(e.g., the year is out of range), then an error is returned.

nodes.Name: MarshalText
nodes.DocComment:
MarshalText implements the [encoding.TextMarshaler] interface. The output
matches that of calling the [Time.AppendText] method.

See [Time.AppendText] for more information.

nodes.Name: UnmarshalText
nodes.DocComment:
UnmarshalText implements the [encoding.TextUnmarshaler] interface.
The time must be in the RFC 3339 format.

nodes.Name: Unix
nodes.DocComment:
Unix returns the local Time corresponding to the given Unix time,
sec seconds and nsec nanoseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC.
It is valid to pass nsec outside the range [0, 999999999].
Not all sec values have a corresponding time value. One such
value is 1<<63-1 (the largest int64 value).

nodes.Name: UnixMilli
nodes.DocComment:
UnixMilli returns the local Time corresponding to the given Unix time,
msec milliseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC.

nodes.Name: UnixMicro
nodes.DocComment:
UnixMicro returns the local Time corresponding to the given Unix time,
usec microseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC.

nodes.Name: IsDST
nodes.DocComment: IsDST reports whether the time in the configured location is in Daylight Savings Time.

nodes.Name: norm
nodes.DocComment:
norm returns nhi, nlo such that

	hi * base + lo == nhi * base + nlo
	0 <= nlo < base

nodes.Name: Date
nodes.DocComment:
Date returns the Time corresponding to

	yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss + nsec nanoseconds

in the appropriate zone for that time in the given location.

The month, day, hour, min, sec, and nsec values may be outside
their usual ranges and will be normalized during the conversion.
For example, October 32 converts to November 1.

A daylight savings time transition skips or repeats times.
For example, in the United States, March 13, 2011 2:15am never occurred,
while November 6, 2011 1:15am occurred twice. In such cases, the
choice of time zone, and therefore the time, is not well-defined.
Date returns a time that is correct in one of the two zones involved
in the transition, but it does not guarantee which.

Date panics if loc is nil.

nodes.Name: Truncate
nodes.DocComment:
Truncate returns the result of rounding t down to a multiple of d (since the zero time).
If d <= 0, Truncate returns t stripped of any monotonic clock reading but otherwise unchanged.

Truncate operates on the time as an absolute duration since the
zero time; it does not operate on the presentation form of the
time. Thus, Truncate(Hour) may return a time with a non-zero
minute, depending on the time's Location.

nodes.Name: Round
nodes.DocComment:
Round returns the result of rounding t to the nearest multiple of d (since the zero time).
The rounding behavior for halfway values is to round up.
If d <= 0, Round returns t stripped of any monotonic clock reading but otherwise unchanged.

Round operates on the time as an absolute duration since the
zero time; it does not operate on the presentation form of the
time. Thus, Round(Hour) may return a time with a non-zero
minute, depending on the time's Location.

nodes.Name: div
nodes.DocComment:
div divides t by d and returns the quotient parity and remainder.
We don't use the quotient parity anymore (round half up instead of round to even)
but it's still here in case we change our minds.

nodes.DocComment: go:linkname legacyTimeTimeAbs time.Time.abs

nodes.DocComment: go:linkname legacyAbsClock time.absClock
